newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: China vetoes U.N. peacekeepers for Guatemala.
newsitem.headline: China vetoes U.N. peacekeepers for Guatemala.

text.p: China late on Friday vetoed sending 155 United Nations peacekeepers to Guatemala because of the Central American country's ties with Taiwan, which it considers a rebel province.
The other 14 Security Council members voted in favor of deploying the military observers to verify a U.N.-brokered peace accord ending 30 years of civil war.
But a negative vote by China -- one of five permanent council members with veto power -- killed the measure. It was the first veto China had cast in nearly 25 years.

China had wanted to wait and continue negotiations with Guatemala but council members decided to embarrass Beijing and force it to veto the measure supported stongly by all states in the Western Hemisphere. Only Russia, which backed the resolution, said the council should not have voted so quickly.
China's ambassador Qin Huasun, in a strongly-worded speech, made clear the Guatemala peace process had nothing to do with his veto.
"The Guatemala authorities cannot expect to have the cooperation of China in the Security Council while taking actions to infringe upon China's sovereignty and territorial integrity," he said.
"No country's peace process should be at the expense of another country's sovereignty and territorial integrity."
But he said if Guatemala would "remove the obstacles" the Chinese government might reconsider the resolution.
Beijing had urged concessions from Guatemala on its diplomatic ties with Taiwan and said a letter from the Central American country on the issue was unsatisfactory.
The vetoed resolution would have given the U.N. peacekeepers a three-month mandate as part of a U.N.-brokered peace plan signed on Dec. 29. in Guatemala City.

Beijing used its Security Council veto on only two previous occasions since taking over the Chinese seat from Taiwan in 1971. The first was on Aug. 25, 1972, to block U.N. membership for Bangladesh. The other was the following month in connection with an amendment to a Middle East resolution.
Guatemala has diplomatic relations with Taiwan, which gives it considerable economic aid.
China also objects to Guatemala's role, along with a number of other small countries, in backing U.N. membership for Taiwan at each General Assembly session since 1993.

Under military provisions of the peace accord, Guatemala's army will redeploy units to specified locations, after which troops from the rebel Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) move to eight assembly points.
The unarmed U.N. military observers were to have verified the cease-fire and patrol assembly points.

Guatemala's ambassador to Washington, Pedro Lamport, told the Council that "abuse of the status of permanent members by misuse of the veto is unacceptable" and that "note must be taken of this by the General Assembly."

U.N. sources said that alternative arrangements, such as getting the Organization of American States to organize peacekeepers, could probably not be completed quickly. This might also jeopardize military demobilization plans.

"We have had extremely positive relationships with Tawian for more than 40 years," Lamport told reporters. "We are not a country which is going to change the friendship immediately. We are not going to change our friendship with Taiwan."
